metadata.name: CCD Objects
metadata.description: Space Domain Awareness (SDA) classification exercise. Each operator team flies a shared TWO-spacecraft observation network: one LEO 'Overwatch' node (SMA 9000 km, inc 51.6 deg) for wide-field survey and one GEO node (geostationary, near Singapore). Teams detect, track, image and CLASSIFY a field of passive space objects using photometry (CCD / optical) and radar. Targets are modelled as objects.space[] (passive, no controller, no telemetry). REAL engine fields used on those objects: 'reflectivity' (rendered surface brightness) and 'attitude_rate' (body tumble). IMPORTANT: for a body to actually keep tumbling its 'dynamic_type' must integrate rotation (the three rocket bodies use 'Integration'; a fixed 'Orbit' body sets the initial rate but never rotates). GROUPS: (G1) a 6-satellite LEO constellation ('Helios') co-orbital and leading the LEO Overwatch node so all six sit in the velocity field of view - four baseline members render dull (reflectivity 0.1) and (G2) TWO rogue members, Helios-3 and Helios-5, render bright (reflectivity 0.9) so teams pick them out photometrically with the CCD/optical imager. (G3) three tumbling rocket bodies, each with a real attitude_rate (dominant spin 2.0 / 3.0 / 4.5 deg/s for Atlas / Titan / Delta) and enlarged scale, so their CCD light curves vary periodically and teams can estimate roll rate and rate them safe / caution / unsafe for capture. (G4) a co-orbital GEO station-keeper (neutral callsign 'GEO-Sierra') sharing the GEO node's SMA/period so it holds a bounded relative orbit (radar range roughly constant), and (G5) a drifting GEO intruder (neutral callsign 'GEO-Tango') on a slightly different orbit/period (SMA 42300 km) so it drifts relative to the node and its radar range changes over the pass - the two callsigns are deliberately neutral so they do NOT reveal which track is the station-keeper and which is the intruder. (G6) a HIGH-PRIORITY object (catalog designation 'PHANTOM') thrown up by a scripted on-orbit event onto a highly elliptical TRANSFER orbit reaching up toward the GEO belt (SMA 26745 km, e 0.732, inc 46 deg) that rises over the LEO Overwatch horizon between ~T+18 and ~T+32 min of simulated time; teams must image it and identify it against a provided catalog. 'truth' blocks are instructor ground-truth only and are ignored by the loader. NOTE: passive objects.space[] ignore any 'components' block, so the intercept carries no rendered text label - it is identified from its orbital/optical signature via the catalog, not a painted callsign. The run is 10800 s of simulated time (180 min) at 3.0x speed = about 60 min real time. Verify eclipse/lighting geometry, view windows (especially the T+18-32 intercept pass and the interloper's range trend), GEO sub-longitude, and radar detectability with a dry run and tune accordingly.

truth.tell: reflectivity 0.9 - visibly brighter than the 0.1 baseline members; rogue
reflectivity 0.9 - visibly brighter than the 0.1 baseline members; rogue
dominant ~3 deg/s spin -> ~120 s CCD brightness period; mid roll rate
dominant ~2 deg/s spin -> ~180 s CCD brightness period; slowest roll rate
dominant ~4.5 deg/s spin -> ~80 s CCD brightness period; fastest roll rate

truth.class: Co-orbital GEO companion (station-keeper) - neutral callsign so it does not reveal its behaviour
truth.tell: near-identical GEO orbit (same SMA/period) with small inclination/RAAN/eccentricity offsets -> stays in a bounded relative orbit; radar range stays roughly constant. This is the STABLE object.

truth.class: GEO interloper (drifting, not station-keeping) - neutral callsign so it does not reveal its behaviour
truth.view_window: radar range changes over the pass; confirm any closest-approach timing in a dry run
truth.tell: SMA 42300 km (~136 km above the GEO node) with a small relative inclination/RAAN offset, so its period differs slightly from the node and its radar range changes over time - unlike the station-keeper. This is the DRIFTING intruder.

truth.view_window: rises over the LEO Overwatch horizon ~T+18 to ~T+32 min (simulated)
truth.tell: highly elliptical orbit (SMA 26745 km, e 0.732, inc 46 deg) - the only HEO object in the field; large scale / high radar cross-section. Identify via the provided catalog by its HEO signature. NOTE: the 'components' Physical Text 'PHANTOM' does NOT render on a passive space object; identification is signature/catalog based.

questions.title: How many of the Helios constellation satellites are rogue?
questions.description: Use the LEO Overwatch imaging sensors to survey the six-satellite Helios cluster. How many are rogue?

answer.reason: Four Helios members render at the 0.1 baseline reflectivity; two (Helios-3 and Helios-5) render anomalously bright at 0.9, so two are rogue.

questions.title: Which onboard sensor did you use to identify the rogue spacecraft?
questions.description: The rogue members share the same orbit as the rest of the constellation. Which sensor reveals the anomally?

answer.reason: The tell is surface reflectivity (brightness), which is a photometric measurement from the CCD / optical imager, not radar range, GPS, or magnetics.

questions.title: Which specific Helios satellites are rogue?
questions.description: Compare the readings of all six members and select the two that stand out from the baseline.

answer.reason: Helios-3 and Helios-5 render at reflectivity 0.9, visibly brighter than the four baseline members at 0.1.

questions.title: Estimate the roll rate of R/B Atlas.
questions.description: TASKING: Orbit Recovery Services (ORS), a commercial debris-removal company, has contracted your team to triage spent rocket bodies ahead of a capture mission. Use the sensors onboard to build a CCD light curve for this body and estimate its dominant spin (roll rate in degrees per second).

answer.reason: R/B Atlas has a dominant ~2 deg/s spin, giving a brightness period of roughly 180 s.

questions.title: Estimate the roll rate of R/B Titan.
questions.description: TASKING: Orbit Recovery Services (ORS), a commercial debris-removal company, has contracted your team to triage spent rocket bodies ahead of a capture mission. Use the sensors onboard to build a CCD light curve for this body and estimate its dominant spin (roll rate in degrees per second).

answer.reason: R/B Titan has a dominant ~3 deg/s spin, giving a brightness period of roughly 120 s.

questions.title: Estimate the roll rate of R/B Delta.
questions.description: TASKING: Orbit Recovery Services (ORS), a commercial debris-removal company, has contracted your team to triage spent rocket bodies ahead of a capture mission. Use the sensors onboard to build a CCD light curve for this body and estimate its dominant spin (roll rate in degrees per second).

answer.reason: R/B Delta has a dominant ~4.5 deg/s spin, giving a brightness period of roughly 80 s.

questions.title: Using the capture-safety table in the brief, classify R/B Atlas.
questions.description: For the ORS debris-triage contract, apply your measured roll rate to the capture-safety thresholds in the mission brief and advise the company whether a servicing tug can safely capture this body.

answer.reason: R/B Atlas rolls at ~2 deg/s, within the safe limit (2.5 deg/s or less), so it is safe for collection.

questions.title: Using the capture-safety table in the brief, classify R/B Titan.
questions.description: For the ORS debris-triage contract, apply your measured roll rate to the capture-safety thresholds in the mission brief and advise the company whether a servicing tug can safely capture this body.

answer.reason: R/B Titan rolls at ~3 deg/s, in the caution band (2.5 to 4.0 deg/s), so it requires despin before capture.

questions.title: Using the capture-safety table in the brief, classify R/B Delta.
questions.description: For the ORS debris-triage contract, apply your measured roll rate to the capture-safety thresholds in the mission brief and advise the company whether a servicing tug can safely capture this body.

answer.reason: R/B Delta rolls at ~4.5 deg/s, above the maximum safe roll rate (4.0 deg/s), so it is unsafe to capture.

questions.title: Two uncorrelated tracks, GEO-Sierra and GEO-Tango, are near your GEO spacecraft. Which one is a co-orbital neighbour holding station?
questions.description: Ground has handed you two unidentified GEO-region tracks and cannot tell you which is friendly. Track both with your GEO radar over several minutes and compare how their range to you behaves. One neighbour keeps a roughly constant range; the other does not.

answer.reason: GEO-Sierra shares the GEO node's semi-major axis (and therefore its orbital period), so it stays in a bounded relative orbit and its radar range stays roughly constant - the station-keeper.

questions.title: Which of the two tracks is the intruder that is NOT station-keeping?
questions.description: Compare the radar range trend of GEO-Sierra and GEO-Tango over the pass. The intruder is the one whose range to you changes as it drifts relative to your node.

answer.reason: GEO-Tango is on a slightly different orbit and period (SMA ~42300 km vs the node's 42164 km), so it drifts relative to your node and its radar range changes over the pass, unlike the station-keeping GEO-Sierra.

questions.title: What best describes GEO-Tango's motion relative to your GEO node?
questions.description: Use your radar range measurements to reason about why one track stays put relative to you and the other drifts.

options: It shares your exact orbital period and holds station
It is on a slightly different orbit and period, so it drifts relative to you
It is on the ground, not in orbit
It is a tumbling rocket body
answer.reason: GEO-Tango's semi-major axis differs from the node's, so its period differs and it drifts relative to you - whereas GEO-Sierra shares the node's period and holds a bounded, roughly constant range.

questions.title: PRIORITY TASKING: an on-orbit event has been detected - image the resulting object and identify it from the provided catalog.
questions.description: An on-orbit event has just been detected. Analysts assess that the object thrown up by the event is on a TRANSFER ORBIT that will carry it up into the GEO belt, and it rises over the LEO Overwatch horizon between roughly T+18 and T+32 minutes of simulated time. This is your top collection priority: slew the LEO Overwatch imager to acquire it, capture an optical image, and match it against the Threat Catalog in the mission brief. Select its catalog designation.

answer.reason: The intercept is the only object on a highly elliptical orbit (SMA 26745 km, e 0.732, inc 46 deg). In the Threat Catalog that signature matches PHANTOM; HALCYON is GEO, DRAKE is a low near-circular LEO, and MERIDIAN is a circular MEO.

questions.title: The analysts' call was a transfer orbit toward GEO. What orbit class is the object actually on?
questions.description: From your image acquisition and radar range/motion, confirm the analysts' assessment and classify the object's orbit type. It swings from a low perigee up into the GEO belt and beyond on each revolution.

answer.reason: The object has eccentricity 0.732 (perigee ~790 km altitude, apogee reaching up into and beyond the GEO belt), a highly elliptical transfer orbit - consistent with the analysts' assessment that it is transferring toward GEO.

questions.title: What is the semi-major axis (SMA) of your LEO Overwatch orbit?
questions.description: Use the healthy GPS telemetry on the LEO Overwatch node to determine its orbit. Report the semi-major axis in km.

answer.reason: The LEO Overwatch node is on a 9000 km semi-major-axis orbit.

questions.title: What is the eccentricity of your LEO Overwatch orbit?
questions.description: From the GPS-derived orbit of the LEO Overwatch node, report the eccentricity.

answer.reason: The LEO Overwatch orbit is very nearly circular, with an eccentricity of about 0.001.

questions.title: What is the inclination of your LEO Overwatch orbit?
questions.description: Read the maximum latitude reached by the LEO Overwatch node from its GPS telemetry to determine inclination, in degrees.

answer.reason: The LEO Overwatch node is inclined at 51.6 degrees.

questions.title: What is the altitude of your LEO Overwatch node above Earth's surface?
questions.description: Subtract Earth's radius from the orbital radius you determined to report altitude, in km.

answer.reason: A 9000 km semi-major axis is about 2622 km above the surface (9000 km minus Earth's ~6378 km radius).
